lesson.title: How things talk
lesson.subtitle: Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, mobile and LoRa, and where your data goes

video.title: How things talk
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talking to the student)

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph at his desk, a small sensor box beside his phone; readings pop up. Cut to the garden fence far away: the phone screen stays empty.
scenes.animation: Readings tick in on the desk; in the garden the phone shows a spinning wait icon.
scenes.narration: My class built a sensor for the school garden. On my desk, it worked perfectly. Out in the garden: nothing. The problem wasn't the sensor. It was how it talked.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how connected things talk, and where your data goes.

scenes.visual: A sensor sends rings of radio waves outwards. Three dials appear beside it: range, battery, data.
scenes.animation: Waves ripple out; each dial pops in as it is named.
scenes.narration: Connected things send what they sense by radio, and every radio makes a trade. How far does it reach? How much battery does it use? How much data can it carry?

scenes.visual: Left: a fitness band linked to a phone across a desk. Right: a router in a house, linking a laptop playing video.
scenes.animation: A short arc links band and phone; wider rings spread from the router.
scenes.narration: Bluetooth reaches about ten to thirty metres, usually to a phone, and sips power. Wi-Fi reaches thirty to fifty metres indoors and carries lots of data, even video, but needs a router and plenty of power.

scenes.visual: Left: a phone mast over a village. Right: a small LoRa box on a fence post, its signal crossing fields to a gateway on a far rooftop.
scenes.animation: Mast bars fill; a thin long arc travels kilometres to the gateway.
scenes.narration: For long distances, a mobile network works anywhere with coverage, but needs a SIM and a data plan. LoRa reaches two to five kilometres in a town, and ten or more in open country. It sends a few dozen bytes at a time, on very little power, to a gateway.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma beside a map: a rain gauge in a field, the farm office 3 km away. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A farm rain gauge sends one small reading an hour to an office three kilometres away, with no power in the field. Which radio?

scenes.visual: The LoRa card lights up; a thin arc carries a tiny packet from the gauge to the office. A battery icon stays nearly full.
scenes.animation: Card glows; the packet travels; the battery barely drops.
scenes.narration: LoRa. Three kilometres is too far for Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, and a reading is only a few bytes. LoRa carries it that far on so little power that a battery lasts a year.

scenes.visual: A number, 28 °C, travels left to right: sensor, gateway box, internet, cloud server, phone app.
scenes.animation: Each stop lights up as the number reaches it.
scenes.narration: Now follow one reading. The sensor sends it to a gateway, which passes radio messages to the internet. The internet carries it to a cloud server, a computer in a data centre. Then an app on your phone shows it.

scenes.visual: The reading passes through four pairs of hands, each labelled. Then a location pin, a microphone and a home camera appear with warning outlines.
scenes.animation: Hands pass the packet along; the private items pop in red.
scenes.narration: At every step, someone else handles your reading: the router's owner, the internet company, the cloud company, the app maker. A garden's temperature is harmless. Your location or your home camera is not.

scenes.visual: The same journey twice: on top, the reading is plain text every hand can read; below, it is locked in a padlocked box until the app opens it.
scenes.animation: A padlock snaps shut on the lower packet; the hands see only scribbles.
scenes.narration: So data should travel encrypted: scrambled, so only the two ends can read it. A website's padlock, https, does exactly that. But the app at the end still reads it all, so choose apps you trust.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph beside a drawing of a home camera, a line of hands and a phone. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Aisha's family camera sends video to an app with no encryption. Who could watch it on the way?

scenes.visual: Four icons line up: a dial, a short arc, a long arc, a padlock.
scenes.animation: Icons line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Anyone on the way could: without encryption, everyone in the middle can see it. Remember: radios trade range, power and data. Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are short; mobile and LoRa go far. And lock your data on the way.

scenes.visual: A student walks round a living room with a notebook, ticking a TV, a router and earbuds; a three-column table: Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, mobile.
scenes.animation: Ticks appear in the table as each device is found.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: a radio hunt at home. List five connected things, like a TV, a router or earbuds. Guess how each talks: Bluetooth, Wi-Fi or mobile. Then check its settings. Next time: mesh networks.

checkpoints.prompt: A farm rain gauge sends a small reading every hour to an office 3 km away. There's no power in the field. Which radio?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — 3 km is too far for Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, and LoRa carries a small reading that far on very little power.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — Bluetooth and Wi-Fi reach tens of metres, not kilometres. LoRa carries small readings kilometres away on very little power.

checkpoints.prompt: A home camera sends video to an app with no encryption. Who could watch it on the way?

options.text: Only the family: it's their camera
Anyone who handles it on the way

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — without encryption, every router and company in the middle could see it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — owning the camera doesn't hide the video. Without encryption, anyone who passes it along could watch.
